SOURCE: "Language Models as Knowledge Bases?", Fabio Petroni, Tim Rocktäschel, Patrick Lewis, Anton Bakhtin, Yuxiang Wu, Alexander H. Miller, Sebastian Riedel (Facebook AI Research / UCL). EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, proceedings pages 2463–2473. Code: https://github.com/facebookresearch/LAMA
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/petroni-2019-language-models-as-knowledge-bases.pdf

COVERAGE: Read all 49,743 of 49,743 chars, from the abstract through the end of the references. The paper has no appendix. I skimmed the references only for where the method comes from. Page numbers below are proceedings pages. PDF page 1 is p.2463, so Table 2 is on PDF p.7 and Figures 3 and 4 are on PDF p.8.

CLAIMS
- claim: With no fine-tuning, BERT-large recalls single-token Wikidata facts from its weights about as well as a KB built by a relation extractor (RE) that was given the sentences stating each fact plus an oracle entity linker. It is slightly better on Google-RE and slightly worse on the T-REx total.
  number: Google-RE total P@1 is 10.5 for BERT-large vs 7.6 for REo and 1.2 for REn. T-REx total P@1 is 32.3 for BERT-large vs 33.8 for REo and 6.1 for REn.
  setup: LAMA probe. Cloze queries are built from hand-written templates. Every model ranks the answer over a shared vocabulary of about 21K case-sensitive tokens, the intersection of all model vocabularies. Answers are single tokens only. The metric is mean P@1 per relation, averaged across relations. Google-RE covers 3 relations and 5,527 facts. T-REx covers 41 relations with at most 1,000 facts each, 34,039 facts in total.
  quote: Table 2 rows "Total 5527 3 4.4 - 1.2 7.6 2.6 1.6 2.0 3.0 9.8 10.5" and "Total 34039 41 22.03 - 6.1 33.8 8.9 18.3 4.7 7.1 31.1 32.3". Text: "obtain a 2 .2 and 2 .9 respective average accuracy improvement over the oracle-based RE baseline."
  where: Table 2, p.2469
- claim: Recall depends strongly on relation type. BERT-large does very well on 1-to-1 relations and poorly on N-to-M relations. On N-M the oracle RE baseline and even the per-relation frequency baseline come close to or beat it.
  number: P@1 by relation type, BERT-large / REo / Freq: 1-1 is 74.5 / 10.0 / 1.78; N-1 is 34.2 / 33.8 / 23.85; N-M is 24.3 / 36.7 / 21.95.
  setup: T-REx. 1-1 has 2 relations and 937 facts, N-1 has 23 relations and 20,006 facts, N-M has 16 relations and 13,096 facts. For N-M, the other valid objects are removed from the ranking, following Bordes et al. (2013).
  quote: "1-1 937 2 1.78 - 0.6 10.0 17.0 36.5 10.1 13.1 68.0 74.5 / N-1 20006 23 23.85 - 5.4 33.8 6.1 18.0 3.6 6.5 32.4 34.2 / N-M 13096 16 21.95 - 7.7 36.7 12.0 16.5 5.7 7.4 24.7 24.3". Text: "the performance of BERT is very high for 1-to-1 relations (e.g., capital of ) and low for N-to-M relations." Intro: "for some relations (particularly N-to-M relations) performance is very poor"
  where: Table 2 and §5 T-REx, p.2469; intro p.2464
- claim: Some fact types are almost never recalled. Dates are close to zero, and BERT does no better than the frequency baseline on them.
  number: birth-date P@1 is 1.4 for BERT-large, 1.9 for Freq and 1.9 for REo. birth-place is 16.1 and death-place is 14.0 for BERT-large.
  setup: Google-RE
  quote: "birth-date 1825 1 1.9 - 0.0 1.9 0.3 1.1 0.1 0.1 1.5 1.4"
  where: Table 2, p.2469
- claim: Compared with retrieve-then-read open-domain QA (DrQA), closed-book BERT-large is far behind at P@1. The gap narrows at P@10.
  number: P@1 is 17.4 for BERT-large vs 37.5 for DrQA. P@10 is 57.1 vs 63.5.
  setup: 305 context-insensitive questions from the SQuAD dev set with single-token answers, rewritten by hand into cloze form. DrQA uses TF-IDF retrieval over Wikipedia plus a neural reader, and its predictions are restricted to single tokens. BERT is not fine-tuned and has no retrieval.
  quote: "SQuAD Total 305 - - 37.5 - - 3.6 3.9 1.6 4.3 14.1 17.4" and "when comparing DrQA and BERT-large in terms of P@10, we ﬁnd that gap is remarkably small (57.1 for BERT-large and 63.5 for DrQA)."
  where: Table 2 p.2469; §5 SQuAD p.2470
- claim: Even when the correct object is not ranked first, it is usually somewhere near the top.
  number: about 60% of answers are in the top 10 and 80% in the top 100.
  setup: T-REx, BERT
  quote: "For BERT, the correct object is ranked among the top ten in around 60% of the cases and among the top 100 in 80% of the cases."
  where: §5, p.2469 (Fig. 2)
- claim: How often the object appears in training data predicts whether the fact is recalled. How often the subject appears does not. Model confidence is the strongest correlate of being correct.
  number: The text gives no correlation values. The heatmap labels in Fig. 3 extract as a P@1 row of "-0.05 0.2 0.42 0.31 0.12 0.035". I read these as SM, OM, LPFP, SOCS, ST, SWP, but the mapping is my reconstruction of the heatmap layout, so verify against the figure before citing the numbers.
  setup: Pearson correlation with BERT-large P@1 on T-REx. Mention counts come from a recreated BERT corpus, because "The original training corpus is not available".
  quote: "the number of times an object is mentioned in the training data positively correlates with performance while the same is not true for the subject of a relation. Furthermore, the log probability of a prediction is strongly positively correlated with P@1. Thus, when BERT has a high conﬁdence in its prediction, it is often correct."
  where: §5, p.2469–2470; Fig. 3 p.2470
- claim: The answer depends on how the query is phrased. The authors treat their single-template results as a lower bound. BERT and ELMo 5.5B vary least across 10 natural phrasings, but they are also the models most likely to have seen those exact sentences in training.
  number: 10 aligned sentences per fact, up to 100 facts per relation. The text gives no variance numbers.
  setup: T-REx, facts with at least 10 alignments
  quote: "for some relations we ﬁnd both worse and better ways to query for the same information ... We argue that this means we are measuring a lower bound for what language models know." Fig. 4 caption: "ELMo 5.5B and both variants of BERT are least sensitive to the framing of the query but also are the most likely to have seen the query sentence during training."
  where: §4.5 p.2468; Fig. 4 p.2470
- claim: When BERT-large is wrong, it usually still predicts an object of the right type.
  number: none
  setup: Table 3, randomly picked examples. Examples: "JDK is developed by ___" gives IBM where the answer is Oracle. "Dani Alves plays with ___" gives Santos where the answer is Barcelona.
  quote: "We ﬁnd that BERT-large generally predicts objects of the correct type, even when the predicted object itself is not correct."
  where: p.2470; Table 3 p.2471
- claim: Commonsense recall from ConceptNet is at a similar level to factual recall.
  number: P@1 is 19.2 for BERT-large and 4.8 for Freq.
  setup: 16 relations, 11,458 facts, with templates taken from OMCS sentences
  quote: "ConceptNet Total 11458 16 4.8 - - - 3.6 5.7 6.1 6.2 15.6 19.2"
  where: Table 2, p.2469
- claim: Adding more text to the relation extraction pipeline did not help it, so the authors suggest LMs trained on growing corpora may come to replace KBs extracted from text.
  number: none. The paper reports only "no significant change".
  setup: WikiText-103 was added to the RE system's data.
  quote: "we added Wikitext-103 as additional data to the re-lation extraction system and observed no signif-icant change in performance."
  where: §6, p.2471

LIMITS
- Only single-token objects are tested, and only the object slot. Multi-token answers, which covers most real entities and dates, are not evaluated. The authors call this "an open challenge".
- Each relation has one hand-written template. The authors concede the results are a lower bound and that results vary with the template.
- Every model ranks over a fixed ~21K-token candidate vocabulary. The models do not generate freely, so this is not open-ended generation or hallucination. The paper says nothing about confident wrong free-text answers.
- On whether BERT-large really "knows" the facts, the authors concede: "this does not mean it does so for the right reasons ... it could have learned associations of objects with subjects from co-occurrence patterns."
- The paper does not study recency or time-bound facts, knowledge cutoff, private or domain data, or updating knowledge. Those are the points a RAG motivation usually needs, and this paper supplies none of them directly.
- The models are dated: BERT 340M, ELMo, Transformer-XL. GPT-2 was excluded because the large model was not public, and GPT-1 because of its lowercased vocabulary. No instruction-tuned or modern LLMs are tested.
- The T-REx alignment is automatic and noisy. The paper reports 97.8% alignment accuracy, citing Elsahar et al. 2018.
- RE-oracle actually beats BERT-large on the T-REx total (33.8 vs 32.3) and on N-M (36.7 vs 24.3). The abstract's word "competitive" covers both directions.

BUILDS ON: Devlin et al. 2018 (BERT); Peters et al. 2018a (ELMo); Dai et al. 2019 (Transformer-XL); Dauphin et al. 2017 (fairseq-fconv); Elsahar et al. 2018 (T-REx); Speer and Havasi 2012 (ConceptNet); Rajpurkar et al. 2016 (SQuAD); Sorokin and Gurevych 2017 (the RE baseline); Chen et al. 2017 (DrQA); Bordes et al. 2013 and Nickel et al. 2016 (rank metrics and filtered N-M ranking); Radford et al. 2019 (GPT-2 zero-shot QA, the closest prior work: "4.1% accuracy on the Natural Questions dataset"); Tenney et al. 2019 and Goldberg 2019 (linguistic probing).

CODE: none in the paper. The repo URL is in the abstract on p.2463.

FIGURES:
- Figure 1 (p.2463, PDF p.1), "Querying knowledge bases (KB) and language models (LM) for factual knowledge." It shows the query (Dante, born-in, X) against a KB next to "Dante was born in [Mask]" against an LM. This is the best candidate for "The knowledge gap": in one picture it shows parametric memory as a lookup and why that lookup can fail.
- Figure 3 (p.2470, PDF p.8), the correlation heatmap. It is the alternative if the note wants to show that frequency drives recall.
- Figure 2 (P@k curves) and Figure 4 (rank distribution under different phrasings) are secondary.

PROBLEMS:
- pypdf printed a fontTools warning, but the text came out clean. Ligatures (ﬁ, ﬀ) and some split numbers ("2 .2") remain.
- The heatmap values in Fig. 3 extract as unlabelled rows of numbers, so the column mapping I gave is a reconstruction.
- The abstract/intro has an internal inconsistency. Intro (iv) says BERT reached "57.1% precision@10 compared to 63.5% of a knowledge base constructed using a task-speciﬁc supervised relation extraction system", but §5 and Table 2 say the 63.5 figure belongs to DrQA (retrieval plus reader), not an RE-built KB. Cite §5, p.2470, for this number.
- The source contains no embedded instructions.
